name: Victor Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big presses at a plastics plant out on Quarry Road. We mould parts for cars: door trim clips, vent housings, the little brackets nobody ever sees. I'm on at six, I walk the line with the night lead, then I spend most of the day on press seven and press nine, the two old 450-tonne machines nobody else can keep happy. When a mould sticks or the parts come out with flash on the edges, they call me, because I can hear it in the cycle before the sensors catch it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm good at it, honestly. Twenty years in, I can set a mould in forty minutes that takes the young guys two hours. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than the plant over in the next county, and the noise, and management asking me to train people for nothing extra. I'm also the shop steward for our section, so half my lunch break is somebody's problem with their rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Every few years someone in a suit comes through with a new system that's going to change everything, and two years later we're still clearing jams by hand. At the union meeting I'd say, good, now let's talk about the pay rise we're actually owed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not happy. Hype or no hype, the company would still use AI as a story to keep wages down. They'd say, be grateful you still have a job, and that line works on people with no savings, which is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my head down on press seven, keep pushing for the cost-of-living raise through the union, and keep doing the overtime Saturdays because that's what pays for the kids' football and the car. Ingrid and I would keep juggling the mortgage the way we do now, month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit tired. It's the same worry I've had for ten years, just with a new label on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company would use it as a story to keep wages down. Has that already happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the plant manager put up a poster about smart factory something, with a robot arm on it. Same month, they told us the raise would be one percent because of investment costs. Nobody's seen the robot arm. We've all seen the one percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's the money worry that's actually on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler. It's fourteen years old and it groans like press nine. If it goes this winter, that's a loan, because we've got maybe three weeks of money in the account. That keeps me up more than any computer.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was hype all along, the same as every new system that comes through the plant. At the union meeting I'd move straight on to the pay rise we're owed.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but still suspicious. I think the company would use AI as an excuse to keep wages low, and that works on people with no savings like me.
S0.do: Keeps working his usual shifts on press seven and Saturday overtime. Keeps pushing for a cost-of-living raise through the union and keeps juggling the mortgage month to month.
S0.feel: Mostly fine but worn down. It's an old worry with a new label.
S0.quote: Nobody's seen the robot arm. We've all seen the one percent.
S0.fieldNote: Victor's worry in the calm scenario isn't the technology but the boss using it as a talking point. His real stress is ordinary and concrete: a fourteen-year-old boiler and three weeks of cash. He hears the plant the way other people hear music, and he's proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in writing: no robot comes onto the floor without a deal on jobs and retraining. I'd say that at the union meeting, and I'd say it louder to the plant manager. Online I don't post much, but I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the presses are the easy bit to automate. A robot arm pulling parts and stacking boxes, that's three jobs on my line gone. They'd keep me longer because I know the old machines, but they'd replace the old machines too, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to push for a technology agreement, so every new robot comes with notice and a say for us. I'd stop the Saturday takeaway and the streaming stuff, and try to put fifty a week aside, even if it only gets us to two months. And I'd vote for whoever promises proper retraining money, not just a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm not scared of losing to a robot on skill, I'm scared of losing to it on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three jobs on your line. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who packs at the end of press nine. She's fifty-six, her English isn't great, and she's the fastest packer we have. There's no course they'd send her on that would land her anything in this town. I'd fight for her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you? Would you go on a course if they offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd go, because I'd be the one telling everyone else to go. But I'd hate it. I'm not a screen person, I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't want to start. I'd sit there thinking, I could be fixing press seven right now.

S1.say: I'd say no robot comes onto our floor without a written deal on jobs and retraining. I'd say it at the union meeting and to the plant manager, and share the union's posts online.
S1.think: I think the packing and stacking jobs on my line go first. They'd keep me a while because I know the old presses, but in the end they'd replace the presses too.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a technology agreement with notice and a say on new robots. Cuts takeaways and streaming to save about fifty a week, and votes for parties promising real retraining money.
S1.feel: Tight and uneasy, more worried about losing on price than on skill.
S1.quote: I'm not scared of losing to a robot on skill, I'm scared of losing to it on price.
S1.fieldNote: His first instinct is to protect others, especially Marta, the older packer. He says he'd go on a retraining course to set an example but admits he'd hate it, which is the clearest sign of how little appetite he has for change. Money is so thin that saving fifty a week counts as a big move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and the government has to step in now, not in five years. Pay people while the robots come in, tax the companies doing it, keep the plants open. I'd be at every meeting and probably on the picket line if they tried to shut us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us? We'd be finished. Two years is nothing. The plant would buy whatever robot cell is going, because the car companies would demand it, and a guy with a two-year diploma and a feel for an old press isn't worth anything once there's no old press. I'd be forty-five with a mortgage and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything right away: the second car goes, the kids' clubs drop to one each, we stop the holiday at Ingrid's sister's. I'd ring the bank about the mortgage before they ring me. And I'd throw myself into the union and the council, because if there's no government help in that first year, my family's living on Ingrid's care-home wage, and that doesn't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor drops out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the second car goes. What else would go, in order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Car, then the phones go to the cheap plan, then the football club for Oskar, which would kill him. After that it's food, and I don't want to think about after that. My dad lost his job at the steelworks when I was eleven and I remember the beans on toast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that dad's work is changing and it isn't their fault or mine. Mia's nine, she'd just want to know if we're keeping the dog. Oskar's twelve and he'd figure out the rest from my face, because I'm a terrible liar.

S2.say: I'd say this is what we warned about and the government must act now: support people's pay, tax the companies, keep plants open. I'd be at every meeting and on the picket line if needed.
S2.think: I think two years is nothing and the plant would buy robot cells fast. I'd be forty-five with a mortgage, a two-year diploma and no job.
S2.do: Sells the second car, drops the kids' clubs and the family holiday, and calls the bank about the mortgage early. Throws himself into union and council campaigns for income support, knowing his partner's care wage can't cover the mortgage alone.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor drops out, with memories of his father's layoff.
S2.quote: My dad lost his job at the steelworks when I was eleven and I remember the beans on toast.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Victor's calm cracks completely. Thin savings, few nearby jobs and no wish to retrain leave him with no plan except the union and the state. The memory of his father's steelworks layoff sits right under the surface and drives a lot of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with a timetable. I'd say we've got five years, so the company and the government had better sit down with the union this year, not in year four. I'd want a plan for every person on the floor written down by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it coming and not enough to get out of the way. I'm not going back to school at forty-five to sit at a screen. I'd be hoping I can hang on, maybe as the guy who babysits the robots, until they don't need a babysitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get our debts down, the credit card first, then try to build three months of cushion, which would be a first for us. I'd push the union hard for a severance deal that's worth something, so if the end comes, there's a lump sum. And I'd talk to Ingrid about her doing more hours, though care homes might get robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way. Like watching a storm come across the fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go back to school, but in the slow one you said you'd go on a course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. A two-week course on the new press, sure, I'd sit it. Going back to college for two years to be something else, no. I know that sounds stubborn. It is stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the five-year version change compared with two years, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm just reacting, cutting and shouting. With five I can at least get the credit card to zero and get the severance deal signed while the company still needs us. That's not nothing. It's not a future either.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so the company and government need to sit down with the union this year. I want a written plan for every person on the floor, by name.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to see it coming but not to get out of the way. I won't go back to school, so I'd hope to hang on as the person who minds the robots.
S3.do: Pays off the credit card in the first two years and tries to build three months of savings. Pushes the union for a strong severance deal while the company still needs workers, and talks with his partner about extra hours.
S3.feel: A slow, steady anxiety, like watching a storm come in.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to see it coming and not enough to get out of the way.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years don't change Victor's goal, which is to stay, but they let him do two practical things: clear debt and lock in severance. When I pointed out the contradiction about courses, he owned it plainly. He draws a hard line between a short course and a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we don't. I'd push for the union to set up a fund and a proper transition plan, and I'd tell younger guys on the line to think hard about what they want to be at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years from now I'm fifty-three. I'd still need to work another twelve years after that. So it's the same end, just later, and I'd have to find something. What I'd really hope is that by then the government's worked out how people live when machines do the work, because I can't see the answer myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first few years I'd pay the mortgage down harder and build a real cushion, six months if I can. Oskar would be starting to think about college, and I'd steer him toward something with people, nursing or teaching, not factories. I'd stay active in the union and keep at the politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Ten years feels like a long time until you remember how fast the last ten went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Oskar when he asks what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, do something where a person wants another person there. I don't know if that's right, but it's what I'd say. He wants to be a game designer, God help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about changing jobs yourself in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at the very end, if someone made it easy, like a council job maintaining something. But I'd want to stay at the plant as long as there's a plant. That's where my people are.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd push the union for a transition fund and plan, and tell younger workers to think hard about where they want to be at fifty.
S4.think: I think it's the same end, just later, and I'd be fifty-three needing another twelve years of work. I'd hope the government works out how people live when machines do the work.
S4.do: Pays the mortgage down harder and aims for six months of savings. Steers his son toward people-based careers like nursing or teaching, and stays active in the union and politics.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, though he knows ten years goes fast.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long time until you remember how fast the last ten went.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Victor's focus shifts from himself to Oskar. He still doesn't plan to retrain and would only move for an easy council job. His trust that collective action and government will find an answer is strong, though he admits he can't see the answer himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. Not because it's worse at the end, it's the same end, but because there's no time to fight for anything. What would help is the government guaranteeing wages for a couple of years while people adjust, paid for by the companies buying the robots. And somebody to keep Marta in work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. I'm the guy they call when press nine's sick. If a robot does that, I'm not just out of money, I'm out of the thing I'm good at. Nobody's got a plan for that bit.

headlineQuote: If a robot does that, I'm not just out of money, I'm out of the thing I'm good at.
portrait: Victor Jensen is a 43-year-old senior press operator at a plastics plant making car parts, and the union shop steward for his section. He's the one they call when the old presses act up, and he hears problems before the sensors do. With about three weeks of money in the bank, a mortgage and two kids, he takes the AI Plateau almost in his stride but sinks fast as the scenarios speed up, reaching panic when AGI arrives in 2 years. He won't retrain or use AI tools, and he puts his faith in the union, government wage support and taxing the companies that bring in robots. More time mainly lets him clear debt, lock in severance and steer his son away from factory work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to fight for anything before the robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A government guarantee of wages for a couple of years while people adjust, paid for by the companies buying the robots, and real help for older coworkers like Marta.
